source.title: PORTER: Language-Grounded Event Representations for Portable Structured EHR Foundation Models
source.authors: L. Guo; A. P. Yan; E. Vettese; Lillian Sung

record.tranche_reason: The study compares downstream AUROC across text-encoder sizes, a different setup from scaling whole language models, and reports results relevant to downstream predictability with scale (V6).
record.gate_note: The study reports held-out pretraining-loss curves for encoder variants, but says the encoder was selected based on validation loss; it does not fit or test power laws in model parameters, tokens, or compute. Those loss curves are not extracted as scaling-law results. The representation-geometry analyses do not measure a claim version.
record.test_reason: This is an EHR foundation-model paper. Its only scale-related result swaps three different frozen text encoders (BioLORD 0.1B, BGE-M3 0.6B, Qwen3-Embedding 8B) into the input pathway of a fixed 115M backbone. It then compares downstream EHR AUROC. That is not a scale series of language models: the encoders differ in family, training data, domain (biomedical vs general) and embedding dimension, and the trained model itself does not change size. So it does not test V6 or any other version. It cites Kaplan et al. only for the 6ND compute approximation. The encoder-size finding is recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that text-encoder scale is not the primary determinant of PORTER performance: 109M BioLORD matched or beat encoders up to 63x larger, most clearly cross-vocabulary. They attribute cross-vocabulary transfer to preservation of patient-level representation geometry. Their main conclusion is that language-grounded event inputs make EHR foundation models portable across vocabularies and sites while matching in-domain performance.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates structured EHR event representations and downstream AUROC, not language-model scaling laws. It varies frozen text-encoder choice rather than sweeping whole-model parameters, training tokens, or compute.
record.method_sensitivity: Downstream AUROC differences varied by evaluation setting: encoder differences were small in-domain and larger in cross-vocabulary transfer; Qwen3 and BGE-M3 were statistically indistinguishable from BioLORD cross-site.

fits_no_version.finding: In a fixed EHR model, swapping a 0.1B biomedical frozen text encoder for general-purpose encoders up to 8B did not improve downstream AUROC. Differences in-domain were small (0.884 vs 0.881) and cross-site was indistinguishable. Cross-vocabulary AUROC was lower for the larger encoders (0.840, 0.818 vs 0.848) and tracked preservation of patient-representation geometry, not encoder size.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Downstream utility of frozen text-encoder embeddings as features in another model depends on domain alignment more than on encoder parameter count.

record.problems: Only three named encoder parameter sizes were compared, while the temporal backbone and training schedule were held fixed; this is not a sweep of whole-model scale. The primary comparison is from one pediatric development site, with one external adult setting.
record.rows_left_out: The Random Embeddings row in Table 3 is omitted because no parameter size is stated for it, so it does not inform the encoder-size comparison. Supplementary Figure S2's held-out loss curves are omitted because the study uses them to select an encoder and does not analyze them as a scaling relationship.

untested.parts: No loss-vs-parameters/tokens/compute sweep or power-law fit.
No compute-optimal allocation analysis; all models are about 1e18 FLOPs.
No depth/width sweep at fixed parameter count.
No scaling of the EHR model; one backbone size only.
No series of language models varying only in scale, and no relation of downstream performance to pretraining loss.
No fitted exponents or fitting-choice analysis.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests'/T2 classification and its V6 labels are dropped. Only three heterogeneous encoders are compared, confounded by domain specialization (BioLORD is biomedical), so no scale-performance relation can be read. The pretraining loss curves in Supplementary Figure S2 compare encoder variants at a fixed backbone size and were used to select BioLORD; they are not a scaling result.

versions.untested_parts: No power-law fits or tests of held-out loss against parameter count, tokens, or compute.
No extrapolation from smaller runs to larger runs.
No compute-budget sweep or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation.
No depth, width, or architecture sweep at fixed parameter count.
No test of a power-law form across modalities or training regimes.
Tests downstream AUROC against the size of the frozen text encoder, not whole-model scale or pretraining loss; only three named encoder sizes and three evaluation settings are compared.
No study of fitted scaling exponents, fit choices, or curves bending away from power laws.

rows.subject: Qwen3
rows.operation_detail: Compared mean downstream AUROC across the 74 in-domain SickKids tasks for a PORTER variant using Qwen3 as its text encoder.
rows.uncertainty: p<0.001 vs BioLORD (two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test, Holm-corrected)
rows.note: The larger encoder's mean AUROC was slightly lower than the BioLORD reference.
rows.check: Frozen-encoder choice inside a fixed EHR model is not language-model scaling, and the encoders are confounded by domain and family. Value 0.881 vs BioLORD 0.884 (p<0.001) is correct but bears on no version.
